p.src: Now the Bodhisattva repeated the spell several times before falling silent, and only then did the demon's pain cease. When he regained his composure and rose to look, he found golden bands around his neck, wrists, and ankles, gripping him painfully; but when he tried to remove them, he could not shift them by so much as a hair. These treasures had already taken root in his flesh, and the more he rubbed them, the more they hurt. Pilgrim laughed. “There, my good boy! The Bodhisattva was afraid you might not grow up properly, so she gave you a collar and bracelets to wear.” Hearing this, the boy flew into another rage, snatched up his spear, and thrust wildly at Pilgrim. Pilgrim hurriedly dodged behind the Bodhisattva and cried, “Recite the spell! Recite the spell!” The Bodhisattva dipped her willow twig in a little sweet dew, sprinkled it toward him, and called, “Close!” At once he dropped his spear and brought both palms together before his chest, unable ever to part them again. This is the origin of the pose known to this day as the Guanyin Twist. Unable to open his hands or wield his spear, the boy finally realized how profound and subtle her divine power was. Having no other recourse, he bowed his head in submission.

p.src: The Bodhisattva invoked a true formula and tilted her pure vase, drawing all that sea of water back into it without leaving a single drop. She said to Pilgrim, “Wukong, this demon has now been subdued, but his wild nature is not yet settled. I shall make him bow at every step until he reaches Mount Luojia, and only then will I release the spell. Hurry back to the cave now and rescue your master.” Pilgrim turned and kowtowed. “You have taken the trouble to journey so far, Bodhisattva. Your disciple ought to escort you part of the way.” The Bodhisattva said, “There is no need to escort me. I fear you may imperil your master's life by delaying.” Pilgrim was delighted to hear this and kowtowed in farewell. The demon soon attained the true fruition, making fifty-three visits in homage to Guanyin.

p.src: Let us say no more for now of how the benevolent Bodhisattva took the boy away. Meanwhile, Sandy had sat waiting in the woods for a long time without seeing Pilgrim return. He loaded the luggage onto the horse, held his demon-subduing staff in one hand and the reins in the other, and emerged from the pine forest to look south, where he saw Pilgrim approaching joyfully. Sandy went to meet him and said, “Brother, why has it taken you until now to return from inviting the Bodhisattva? I have been worried to death.” Pilgrim replied, “You must still be dreaming! Old Sun has already brought the Bodhisattva and subdued the monster.” Pilgrim then gave him a full account of the Bodhisattva's divine powers. Sandy was overjoyed. “Let us go and rescue Master!”

p.src: Master and disciples emerged from the cave, mounted horse and saddle, found the main road, and steadfastly headed west. After travelling for more than a month, they suddenly heard the thunderous sound of water. Tripitaka exclaimed in alarm, “Disciples, where is that sound of water coming from now?” Pilgrim laughed. “You are far too suspicious, old master. You are hardly fit to be a monk. Of the four of us together, why is it only you who hears some sound of water? Have you forgotten the Heart Sutra again?” The Tang Monk replied, “The Heart Sutra was transmitted to me orally by the Crow's Nest Chan Master of Mount Futu. It comprises fifty-four lines and two hundred and seventy characters. I received it by ear then and have recited it constantly ever since. p.src: The Tang Monk dismounted and asked, “Disciples, why is this water so muddy and black?” Bajie said, “Someone must have tipped a vat of indigo into it.” Sandy said, “No, someone must have washed their brushes and inkstones here.” Pilgrim said, “Stop making wild guesses and think of a way to get Master across.” Bajie said, “It would be easy enough for old Pig to cross this river. Whether I rode a cloud or entered the river and pushed through the water, I would be across in less time than it takes to eat a meal.” Sandy said, “If it were old Sandy, I too could mount a cloud or tread the water and cross in an instant.” Pilgrim said, “It is easy for us; only Master presents a difficulty.” Tripitaka asked, “Disciples, how wide is this river?” Bajie replied, “I reckon it is about ten li wide.” Tripitaka said, “The three of you decide which one shall carry me across.” Pilgrim said, “Bajie can carry you.” Bajie said, “I cannot carry him. If I took him on my back and tried to mount a cloud, I could not rise even three feet from the ground. As the saying goes, ‘A mortal carried on the back weighs as much as a mountain.’ And if I carried him while pushing through the water, his weight would drag even me beneath the surface.”

p.src: As master and disciples stood by the river discussing what to do, they saw a man upstream rowing a small boat down toward them. The Tang Monk said delightedly, “Disciples, a boat is coming. Call to him to ferry us across.” Friar Sand called loudly in a stern voice, “Boatman! Come ferry some travelers across! Come ferry us across!” The man in the boat replied, “This is not a ferry. How can I take passengers across?” Friar Sand said, “Whether in Heaven or on earth, nothing comes before helping others. Though yours is not a ferry, we are not travelers who will trouble you time and again. We are Buddhist pilgrims commissioned by the emperor of the Eastern Land to fetch the scriptures. Be so kind as to ferry us across, and you shall have our thanks.” Hearing this, the man rowed close to the bank, steadied himself on his oar, and said, “Master, my boat is small and your party large. How can I take all of you across?” Tripitaka stepped forward to look and saw that the boat was carved from a single length of timber, with only one small well amidships and room for no more than two passengers. “What are we to do?” asked Tripitaka. Friar Sand replied, “In that case, let him take us across in two trips.” Pig, scheming to shirk his work while winning favor, said, “Wujing, you and Elder Brother stay on this bank and watch the luggage and horse. Let me escort Master across first, and then the boat can return for the horse. Elder Brother can leap across by himself.” Monkey nodded. “What you say makes sense.”

p.src: On the bank, Friar Sand and Monkey cried in alarm, “What are we to do? Our old master meets disaster at every step. No sooner had he escaped one demonic trial and enjoyed a fortunate stretch of peaceful travel than he encountered this tribulation in the Black Water.” Friar Sand asked, “Could the boat have capsized? Let us search downstream.” Monkey replied, “It did not capsize. If it had, Pig can swim and would certainly have protected Master and borne him up out of the water. I noticed just now that the boatman had an unwholesome air. He must be the wretch who raised the wind and dragged Master underwater.” Hearing this, Friar Sand said, “Brother, why did you not say so sooner? Watch the horse and luggage while I go underwater to search for them.” Monkey said, “There is something unnatural about the color of this water. I fear you may not be able to enter it.” Friar Sand replied, “How can this water compare with my River of Flowing Sands? I can go, I can go.”

p.src: The worthy monk removed his short robe, bound his arms and legs for action, swung up his demon-subduing treasure staff, and with a splash parted a path through the water. Diving beneath the waves, he strode forward with great steps. As he went, he suddenly heard voices. Friar Sand slipped aside and peered out secretly. Over yonder stood a pavilion, and above its gate were inscribed eight large characters: “Mansion of the Black Water River God, Hengyang Valley.” Then he heard the monster seated within say, “I have labored long, and only today have I obtained my prize. This monk is a good man who has cultivated his virtue through ten incarnations. Anyone who eats even one piece of his flesh will attain longevity and never grow old. I too have waited long for his sake, and this morning my ambition has at last been fulfilled.” He ordered, “Underlings, quickly carry out the iron cage. Steam these two monks whole, then prepare an invitation for my Second Uncle and ask him here to celebrate his birthday in advance.” When Friar Sand heard this, he could no longer contain the fire in his heart. He drew his treasure staff and battered wildly at the gate. He cursed aloud, “You insolent creature! Bring out my master, the Tang Monk, and my senior brother Pig at once!” The fiends inside were so frightened that they hurried away to report, “Disaster!” The old monster asked, “What disaster?” A lesser demon replied, “Outside is a monk with an ill-favored dark face. He is striking the front gate, shouting abuse, and demanding that we hand over the captives!”

p.src: The monster shouted, “Who is out here battering my gate?” Friar Sand replied, “You ignorant, insolent monster! Why did you employ your deceptions, turn yourself into a boatman, and bring my master here in your boat? Return him at once, and I will spare your life.” The monster laughed aloud. “This monk has no notion of life or death. I did capture your master, and now I mean to steam him and invite a guest to the feast. Come up here and let us see which of us is the better fighter. If you can withstand me for three bouts, I shall return your master; but if you cannot, I shall steam and eat you along with him, and you can forget all thought of reaching the Western Heaven.” Enraged by these words, Friar Sand swung his treasure staff and struck straight at the monster’s head; the monster raised his steel whip and hastily parried the blow. Thus the two fought beneath the water—a splendid battle indeed:

p.src: Friar Sand leaped out of the water in a fury and said when he saw Monkey, “Brother, that monster is outrageous!” Monkey asked, “You were down there a long time before coming out. What sort of fiend is it exactly? Did you find Master?” Friar Sand replied, “There is a pavilion down there, and above its gate are written eight large characters: ‘Mansion of the Black Water River God, Hengyang Valley.’ I hid to one side and heard him talking within. He ordered his underlings to scrub the iron cage, intending to steam Master and Pig, then invite his uncle to celebrate his birthday in advance. I flew into a rage and went to batter his gate. The monster came out carrying a jointed steel whip and fought me for a good while—some thirty rounds, I should say—without either of us prevailing. Then I pretended to be defeated, meaning to lure him out so that you could help me fight him. But the monster is remarkably cunning. He would not pursue me and cared only about going back to prepare invitations for his guests. That is why I have only just come back up.” Monkey said, “I wonder what sort of fiend it is.” Friar Sand replied, “Its appearance was rather like a huge soft-shelled turtle; if not that, then it must be some kind of alligator-dragon.” Monkey said, “I wonder who this uncle of his might be.”

u.src: When the Pilgrim and Monk Sha saw him, they said, “You wretch, you have disobeyed your orders.
Your uncle originally placed you here to live, instructing you to cultivate your nature and preserve yourself until the day you made a name, when you would be appointed elsewhere.
Why did you forcibly occupy the Water God's residence, rely on your power to commit violence, deceive your own conscience and your superiors, and use trickery to ensnare my master and junior brother?
I would like to give you one blow, but Old Sun's cudgel is exceedingly heavy; even the lightest tap would end your life.
Where have you confined my master?”
The monster repeatedly knocked his head on the ground and said, “Great Sage, this little terrapin did not know your illustrious name.
Just now I defied my cousin, flaunting my strength against all reason, and he captured me.
Now that I behold the Great Sage, I am infinitely grateful for your mercy in sparing my life.
Your master is still bound inside the water palace. I beg the Great Sage to remove my iron chain and free my hands, so that I may enter the river and bring him out.”
Mo'ang said from beside him, “Great Sage, this wretch is a rebellious fiend and exceedingly treacherous. If you release him, I fear he will conceive some wicked scheme.”
Monk Sha said, “I know the place. Let me go and find Master.”

p.src: The two of them plunged into the water and went straight to the gates of the underwater palace. There the gates stood wide open, without so much as a single lesser guard in sight. They went directly into the pavilions within and found Tripitaka and Eight Rules bound there stark naked. Friar Sand hurriedly untied his master, while the River God freed Eight Rules; each took one of them on his back, rose from the water, and went straight to the bank. When Zhu Eight Rules saw the monster bound in chains nearby, he hastily snatched up his rake and stepped forward to strike, cursing, “You vile beast! So, will you not eat me now?” Pilgrim seized hold of him and said, “Brother, spare his life for now, out of regard for worthy Ao Shun and his son.” Mo'ang stepped forward and saluted, saying, “Great Sage, this humble dragon dares not linger here. Now that your master has been rescued, I shall take this wretch to see my father. Though the Great Sage has spared him from death, my father will certainly not spare him from punishment. He will surely pass judgment and deal with him, after which I shall report back to the Great Sage and offer our apologies.” Pilgrim said, “If that is so, take him away. Give my warmest regards to your honored father; I shall thank him in person when the opportunity arises.” The crown prince escorted the vicious monster into the water and, leading the sea troops, returned directly to the Western Ocean; of this no more need be said.

p.src: Now the God of the Black Water River thanked Pilgrim, saying, “Great Sage, it is entirely through your kindness that I have regained my underwater palace.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, we are still on the eastern bank. How are we to cross this river?” The River God said, “Reverend Sir, do not worry. Please mount your horse; this humble deity will clear the way and lead you across the river.” Only then did the master mount the white horse. Eight Rules took hold of the reins, Friar Sand shouldered the luggage, and Sun Pilgrim attended them on either side. The River God then worked a spell to hold back the waters, damming the upstream flow. In a moment the water below drained away, revealing a broad road. Master and disciples crossed to the western side, thanked the River God, climbed the bank, and continued on their way. And so it was that:
